title: What soil is made of
teaches: What is in a handful of soil, the three sizes of mineral grain, and how their mix decides what a bed is like to garden

blocks.text: Pick up a handful of good garden soil. Less than half of it is rock. About **half** of its volume is solid: tiny broken pieces of rock, the [[minerals|mineral]], with a little [[organic matter|organic]] mixed through, the remains of plants and animals at every stage of rotting. The other half is not there at all. It is the gaps between the grains, the **pores**, and they are shared between [[water|water]] and [[air|air]].

blocks.caption: A handful of loam, by volume, a day after a good soaking

blocks.text: Roots need both halves of that empty space. They drink from the films of water on the grains and breathe from the air between them. A root sitting in pores full of water for days drowns; one in pores full of air dries out. Most of what this course is about, from digging to compost, comes back to keeping that space open and about half full.

The organic part is small, often only 2 to 6 parts in a hundred, but it does far more than its share. It feeds the life in the soil, glues grains into crumbs, and holds water and nutrients like a sponge. Lesson 5 is about it. This lesson is about the other solid part: the minerals.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Good soil is about half solid and half pore space.
The pores hold the [[water|water]] and the [[air|air]] that roots need: roughly half and half once a soaking has drained.

blocks.text: The mineral part comes in three sizes, sorted by how wide each grain is. [[Sand|sand]] is anything from 2 mm down to 0.05 mm, big enough to see and to feel as grit. [[Silt|silt]] is smaller, down to 0.002 mm, too fine to see one by one: dry, it feels like flour. [[Clay|clay]] is smaller still, and its grains are flat plates, sticky when wet and hard as brick when dry. Anything bigger than 2 mm is gravel and stones, and doesn't count.

blocks.caption: The three sizes, blown up so that a clay plate is the size of a pea

blocks.text: Size matters because of **surface**. Break a grain into smaller pieces and the pieces have more surface between them than the grain had. A teaspoon of some clays has as much surface as a football field, and water clings to surfaces, and so do many plant nutrients. That is why [[clay|clay]] holds water and food, and [[sand|sand]] lets both run straight through.
You can measure your own soil's mix with nothing but a jar. The sizes settle out of water at very different speeds: a sand grain sinks like a stone, while a clay plate can hang in the water for days.

blocks.caption: The jar test: shake soil up in water and let it settle
blocks.task: Let the jar settle until you can read all three layers

blocks.text: To try it, fill a straight-sided jar a third full of soil from the bed, with stones and roots picked out. Top it up with water to near the brim, add a teaspoon of dish soap to help the grains come apart, and shake it hard for a few minutes. Mark the side of the jar at the top of the [[sand|sand]] after a minute, at the top of the [[silt|silt]] after six hours, and at the top of the [[clay|clay]] when the water clears, a day or two later. Bits of [[organic matter|organic]] float, so skim them off. Each layer's height over the whole is its share of the mix.

The mix of the three sizes is the soil's **texture**, and soil scientists name it from a triangle. Each corner is all of one size; a point inside is a mix. Twelve regions of the triangle each have a name, from sand to clay, and in the middle is **loam**: a mix in which none of the three takes over, roughly two parts [[sand|sand]], two of [[silt|silt]] and one of [[clay|clay]].

Look at how the regions are shaped. It takes 85 parts in a hundred of [[sand|sand]] for a soil to be called sand, but only 40 of [[clay|clay]] for it to be one of the clays, whatever the rest is. A little clay goes a long way, because its tiny plates fill the gaps between bigger grains and give the whole soil their stickiness.

blocks.title: What texture means in the bed
points: **Sandy** soils drain fast and warm early in spring, but dry out quickly and let nutrients wash away.
**Loamy** soils hold water and nutrients and still let air in: what most vegetables want.
**Clayey** soils hold water and nutrients well, but drain slowly, pack hard and are slow to warm.

blocks.text: Texture is the one thing about a soil you can't change in a season. Turning a clay bed into a loam by digging in sand would take tonnes of it, and too little sand makes clay more like concrete, not less. What you *can* change is how the grains are put together and what lives among them: the soil's structure, which is the next lesson, and its organic matter, which improves sandy and clay soils alike.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on what soil is made of

items.question: This bed dried out and cracked into plates like these. What is it rich in?
items.why: Clay plates shrink as they dry and swell when wet, so a clay soil cracks in a drought. Sand doesn't shrink at all.

items.question: In a jar test, which layer settles first?
items.why: The biggest grains sink fastest: sand is down in about a minute, silt over a few hours, and clay can take a day or two.

items.question: Rubbed between wet fingers, a pinch of soil feels gritty. What is it mostly?
items.why: Sand grains are big enough to feel one by one. Silt feels smooth and silky, clay sticky.

items.question: Roughly how much of a good garden soil, by volume, is pore space?
items.why: About half of a healthy soil is pores, shared between water and air. Pack it down and that share shrinks.

items.question: A jar test gives 70% sand, 20% silt and 10% clay. What will the bed be like?
options: Quick to drain, and in need of watering more often
Slow to drain, and sticky after rain
items.why: That is a sandy loam. It drains and warms quickly, but holds less water and fewer nutrients than a loam.

items.question: Why do most vegetables do best in a loam?
options: It holds water and nutrients but still drains and lets air in
It is the richest in clay
It has no pore space to dry out
items.why: In a loam no one size takes over: the sand keeps it open, the clay holds water and nutrients, and the silt sits between.

items.question: Your clay bed drains slowly. What happens if you dig in a few bags of sand?
options: Very little, or it packs harder
It drains like a sandy soil
items.why: A few bags barely move the mix, and sand in clay can set hard. Organic matter, worked in or laid on top, is what opens up a clay soil.

learned: Soil is about half solid (minerals and a little organic matter) and half pores, shared by water and air.
Sand, silt and clay are the three sizes of mineral grain; the smaller the grain, the more water and nutrients it holds.
A jar test measures the mix, and the texture triangle names it.
Texture can't be changed in a season, but structure and organic matter can.
